title: A Survey of Query Routing Between Semantic and Knowledge-Graph Retrieval for Retrieval-Augmented Generation
content: Retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) systems increasingly hold two kinds of external memory: dense vector indexes over text chunks and knowledge graphs (KGs) extracted from the same corpus. Semantic (vector) retrieval is cheap and strong on single-fact lookup; graph retrieval targets multi-hop, relational and corpus-level questions but, depending on design, can consume up to several hundred times more prompt tokens per query plus a costly indexing stage, and it frequently underperforms plain semantic (vector) RAG on simple questions. A growing body of work therefore routes each query to the backend that suits it. This survey is, to our knowledge, the first dedicated to routing between semantic (vector) and graph retrieval. We formalise routing as cost-aware action selection and define oracle headroom and routing regret. We propose a four-axis taxonomy (routing signal, routing time, decision type and learning paradigm) and review routers, structure and source selectors, and the adaptive-retrieval methods they build on. From the full texts of the core papers we extract and compare reported accuracy, latency, token and indexing costs. Our analysis yields eight findings. Three stand out. First, semantic (vector) and graph retrieval are strongly complementary: oracle routing exceeds the best fixed backend by 21.5 points on RAGRouter-Bench and by 55% relative Hit@1 on STaRK-MAG. Second, current routers recover little of that headroom: about 20% on the only dedicated benchmark, and their gains over the best fixed backend are often under one point. Third, whether a query benefits from the graph depends less on hop count than on answer scope, relation type, temporal constraints and the KG's coverage of the query's entities. We close with a reporting protocol and open problems, including corpus-aware and post-retrieval routing, label bias and access control in hybrid stores.
